t: Find a Peak Element II — Binary Search on Columns
o: A peak is a cell strictly greater than its four orthogonal neighbors; adjacent cells are never equal and the virtual -1 border means a peak always exists, but ANY peak is acceptable. Example 1 (mat = [[1,4],[3,2]]): both 3 and 4 qualify, so [1,0] and [0,1] are both accepted. Example 2 (mat = [[10,20,15],[21,30,14],[7,16,32]]): 30 at (1,1) and 32 at (2,2) are peaks. The required O(m log n) or O(n log m) bound rules out scanning every cell (O(mn)) and points directly at the classic column-wise binary search: probe one middle column per step, discard half the grid, and finish with the row-maximum of the surviving column.
k: Take r = argmax down the probed middle column; comparing mat[r][mid] against only its RIGHT neighbor decides which half of the grid still contains a guaranteed peak.

If mat[r][mid+1] > mat[r][mid], the maximum cell of the right strip [mid+1..hi] cannot be beaten by any neighbor: in-strip neighbors are smaller by maximality, and column-mid neighbors are capped because every value in column mid is <= mat[r][mid] < mat[r][mid+1].
Each iteration reads one column (O(m)), giving O(m log n) total; swapping rows for columns gives the O(n log m) variant.

a.i: Test each cell against its existing neighbors and return the first peak found. Trivially correct and worth mentioning as a baseline; it violates the required complexity bound on large grids.
s: Iterate rows top to bottom, columns left to right.
Compare the current cell with the up/down/left/right neighbors that exist.
Return [i, j] on the first cell greater than all of them.
a.t: O(m x n) — each of the mn cells performs O(1) neighbor checks.

a.i: Probe the middle column and let r be the row containing that column's maximum. If mat[r][mid+1] > mat[r][mid], a peak must exist strictly to the right of mid — take the maximum cell of the strip [mid+1..hi]: its in-strip neighbors are not larger by maximality, and any neighbor in column mid is at most mat[r][mid], which just lost the comparison. Otherwise the column maximum beats its right neighbor and, as a row-max, also beats its left neighbor, so it anchors a peak within [lo..mid]. When the window narrows to a single column, its maximum is a genuine peak.
s: While lo < hi: mid = midpoint; find r maximizing mat[r][mid].
If mat[r][mid] < mat[r][mid + 1], set lo = mid + 1; otherwise set hi = mid.
After the loop find r maximizing mat[r][lo] and return [r, lo].
a.t: O(m log n) — each of about log n steps scans one column of height m.

w: Present the brute force first, then the column binary search; interviewers probe two details: comparing strictly (never >=) and taking the COLUMN MAXIMUM before comparing, which is what makes discarding half the grid safe. Common bugs: comparing whole columns against each other instead of using the row-max anchor, or forgetting the perimeter guarantee that peaks always exist. The symmetric row-wise version achieves O(n log m); pick whichever dimension is smaller. Follow-up: count or list all peaks (much harder), or handle grids where equal adjacent values are allowed.
